description: The best team in the world
summary:
ARES MISSION is a web-based Martian Map that turns scattered NASA data into one clear EVA decision: where to go, why, when, and whether it is safe. Tools like Mars Trek serve regional views; a crew on a Marswalk needs a hyperlocal map for a single excursion.

For six candidate sites (Gale, Jezero, Mawrth Vallis, Meridiani Planum, Columbia Hills, East Melas) or a crew's own data, ARES layers HiRISE terrain and imagery, CRISM minerals, THEMIS thermal inertia, EMARS atmospheric reanalysis, and, at Gale, Curiosity RAD radiation and CheMin drill results as ground truth.

ARES does not just display layers. It scores the terrain against NASA's Moon to Mars objectives, picks the best science targets, and plans an A* route that accounts for slope, wind exposure and dust visibility. It budgets time, suit oxygen (Pandolf model at Mars gravity) and rover energy, finds the best departure hour, and gives a GO/NO-GO based on a 1.5x supply margin and weather and radiation flight rules.

The same plan then drives a first-person helmet or rover HUD that tracks oxygen, suit battery and weather, warns of a suit leak, dust storm or solar particle event, and re-plans the way home on ABORT.
details:
What it does and how it works

ARES Mission turns orbital and rover data from several NASA missions into a single 3D planning and navigation tool for a human Marswalk.

1. Choose a site and goals. Crews choose Gale crater, Jezero crater, or a custom site built from their own files in the browser. They then select science objectives (water, habitability/life, resources, climate history).

2. Find science targets. MRO CRISM summary parameters, HiRISE terrain and THEMIS thermal inertia are combined into a science-value layer scored against NASA's Moon to Mars objectives. ARES picks the stops that best match the chosen goals. CRISM is treated as a guide to candidate sites for later scanning and sampling, not as measured composition.

3. Plan a safe route. A Python pipeline runs A* search on a cost map built from slope. Walking speed uses Tobler's hiking function with a suit factor, oxygen use uses the Pandolf metabolic model scaled to Mars gravity, and rover travel uses speed and Wh/km energy models.

4. Check the weather. At Gale, hourly dust opacity, wind and temperature from the EMARS reanalysis (NASA Ames Mars GCM with TES/MCS assimilation) change the cost map. High dust lowers the safe slope limit and strong wind pushes the route onto sheltered ground. ARES also recommends the best departure hour. Three real Mars-year scenarios are included: a clear season, a dusty season and the 2007 global dust storm.

5. Decide GO / NO-GO. The plan is GO only if supplies (O2, battery, time) exceed needs by a safety factor of at least 1.5 and the weather is within flight rules.

6. Rehearse and execute. A first-person helmet HUD (on foot) or rover HUD shows O2 reserve, suit battery, elapsed time, next waypoint, distance, grade ahead, Mars weather and space weather. A first-person helmet HUD (on foot) or rover HUD shows the astronaut's vital signs ([e.g. heart rate, body temperature]), O2 reserve, suit battery, elapsed time, next waypoint, distance, grade ahead, Mars weather and space weather. Solar particle events and suit leaks can be injected, and ABORT computes a route back to the habitat.

At Gale, Curiosity's traverse (NASA MMGIS) and CheMin drill results (NASA PDS; clay data from Thorpe et al. 2022) appear as a separate ground-truth layer, so users can compare orbital predictions with measured mineralogy.

Benefits

- One view instead of many: terrain, mineralogy, thermal properties, weather and rover ground truth in one place.

- A quantitative, explainable GO/NO-GO decision based on physical models, not only a map.

- Crews can rehearse an EVA, including emergencies, before stepping outside.

- Reusable: any site with a DEM and CRISM data can be loaded through the custom-site builder.

Intended impact

ARES is designed first for the crews who will make the first human Marswalks, and for the mission planners who prepare them. As a Martian settlement grows, the same system can serve as a daily suit HUD for residents and as navigation for surface vehicles. On Earth it can support analog-mission training and give students and the public a hands-on way to explore real NASA Mars data.

Tools and technologies

- Front end: JavaScript (ES modules), Three.js r160 / WebGL for 3D terrain and the first-person HUD, HTML/CSS. Runs in any modern browser, no install.

- Data pipeline: Python (A* route planning, cost maps, physiological and rover models, science scoring) [add libraries, e.g. NumPy, rasterio, GDAL].

- Data: HiRISE DEM (1 m source, shown at 16 m) and USGS Astrogeology HiRISE colour mosaic; MRO CRISM; THEMIS; Curiosity CheMin (PDS) and traverse (MMGIS); EMARS reanalysis; DONKI-format space weather (sample data in this build).

- Hosting: aresmission.us [add host and GitHub link].

How it is creative

Most Mars maps show where things are. ARES answers whether a crew can get there and back, and when. It links science targets, human physiology, vehicle energy and weather into one plan, then lets the user live that plan in first person from inside the helmet, with their own vital signs and life support on screen..

Factors we considered

- Safety first: a 1.5x consumable margin, weather flight rules and an always-available abort route.

- Scientific honesty: the app marks what is measured, estimated or excluded. The imagery is processed colour, not true colour. The GCM cell (about 300 km) is larger than the 10 km map, so weather is one value per hour. Space weather is sample data. Soft soil, boulders and radiation dose are not yet modelled.

- Scale: the 1 m DEM is resampled to a 16 m grid so it runs smoothly in a browser.

- Usability: simple controls, GO/NO-GO at a glance, and touch support.
